title: Knitted pillbox hat
subtitle: A flat-topped structured pillbox hat worked in two pieces and seamed.
excerpt: A knitted pillbox hat with a flat top disc and straight side wall, worked in DK wool on 4 mm needles. The top is worked flat and seamed to the circular side wall, fitting adult heads of 54 to 58 cm.
sourceNotes: Pillbox hats appear in 1950s and 1960s knitting publications. Weldon's Practical Knitter includes flat-crowned hat constructions from the 1900s onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: A method of knitting a small circumference on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the work at the halfway point.
An increase that lifts the horizontal strand between two stitches and knits through the back loop to form a new stitch without a hole.

content.text: This knitted pillbox hat is worked in two pieces: a circular side wall worked in the round, and a flat top disc worked outward from a small centre cast-on. The two pieces are seamed at the top edge. Fits adult heads of 54 (56, 58) cm.

The two-piece construction is chosen because a flat top cannot be achieved with standard crown decreases -- the decreases naturally produce a rounded shape. Working the top as a separate disc gives the clean right angle that defines the pillbox silhouette. The
method works the side wall in the round. About 90 g (200 m) of DK wool. Sits flat on the crown of the head.

items.name: 3.5 mm circular needle, 80 cm (UK 9 / US 4) -- for brim

content.text: 22 sts x 30 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. A pillbox must fit precisely because the side walls are straight with no stretch. At 23 sts per 10 cm the side wall is 2 cm too tight at the brow. Check gauge before starting.
k2tog -- knit two together, right-leaning decrease
Before you cast on, circle your size -- every count reads S (M, L).

on the 3.5 mm needle, cast on 116 (120, 128) sts using long-tail cast-on. Tail formula: tail_cm = (needle mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For size L on a 3.5 mm needle: (3.5 x 128) / 10 + 15 = 60 cm; round up to 65 cm. Join without twisting, place BOR marker. Work 6 rounds k1 p1 rib. Switch to 4 mm needle. Work in stocking stitch until side wall measures 8 cm from cast-on edge. After the side wall, you should have 116 (120, 128) stitches on the needle. Cast off all sts.
Cast on 8 sts and divide evenly onto double-pointed needles or use magic loop. Join. Place marker. Increase round: *k1,

; repeat from * to end. To work m1r: lift the horizontal strand between the stitch on the right needle and the stitch on the left needle from front to back; knit through the back loop. Work increase rounds every other round, with plain rounds between, until the disc measures 17 cm in diameter. Cast off all sts loosely.

Pin the disc to the top edge of the side wall with right sides facing outward. Sew together with mattress stitch, working through one stitch from each piece alternately around the full circumference. Join and fasten off on the inside.

Top disc is too large and buckles at the seam: disc circumference must match the side wall cast-off edge exactly. Measure the disc edge and the side wall top edge before seaming; adjust by adding or removing a few increase rounds.

Seam is visible from the outside: mattress stitch was worked through the wrong legs of the stitches. Work mattress stitch through the outside edge of each stitch, not through the whole stitch, to keep the seam invisible.
Side wall flares at the brim: the brim rib section was worked on a needle that is too large. Go one size down from the main needle for the rib.
Weave in all ends. Wet-block over a cylindrical object (a tin or wide mug) that matches the target head circumference. Pin the top flat and allow to dry completely before removing.
Hand wash cool. Re-block over a cylindrical form to maintain the flat top and straight sides.
The knitted beret applies the same top-disc technique but curves the disc outward to a wide, draping shape rather than keeping it flat.
